doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Wanting to belong: a Jewish kid finding his place in the jazz world
summary: Israels says his early bass thinking was about joining the community and music he loved, as a white middle-class Jewish kid who did not drink or smoke pot.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Did you have a philosophy, a form of philosophy about bass playing in your early career?

It’s an interesting question, I’m not sure that I had anything so that I could call myself formed enough to have a philosophy. I think I was very much wanting to be a member of the club that included people, that was populated by people many of whom didn’t look like me, and who had a cultural milieu, a musical milieu that attracted me so deeply, that felt so much like me that I wanted to belong in it. So whatever I was thinking about playing was focused on how I could play, to be part of that group of people and be part of that music. So I don’t think it was particularly focused on how am I, what kind of personal individual contribution I could make so much as how can I be, how can I join this and be accepted, and be part of it.
Was part of it trying to find your way in the culture of it? Not just the playing but the nightlife and the language and the camaraderie.

Absolutely. And I had to do that in my own personal way. White, middle class Jewish kid from an educated family, hanging out with other quite smart people but whose smarts were oriented in slightly different ways from mine and some of whom were drinking and smoking pot and I wasn’t ready for any of that. So I had to figure out how to be in it and a part of it without, well I had to find a way to fit in. And interestingly it was a pretty wide open society of people that would accept me being there, even though I wasn’t doing everything that some of the other people were doing. I wasn’t alone of course, there were other people like me. I grew up playing with Steve Kuhn and Arnie Wise, another couple of Jewish kids that were attracted to the music.
